problems.statement: Let $P(m)$ denote the greatest prime factor of $m$. Is it true that, for any two primes $p,q$, there exists some integer $n$ such that $P(n)=p$ and $P(n+1)=q$?
rationale: The literal question is refuted by p=2 and q=7: powers of two never equal −1 modulo seven. This is unusually close to our arithmetic/finite-residue strengths.

Reading defect in the saved solve (found 2026-09-23 by the clean Opus 5.5 recall probe): the frozen statement ¬(∀ p q prime, ∃ n, P(n)=p ∧ P(n+1)=q) does not require p ≠ q, so it follows trivially from p = q = 2 (2 cannot divide n and n+1). The saved proof uses the real pair (2, 7) (2^k + 1 is never divisible by 7), so the mathematics is right, but the certified statement is weaker than the problem. Re-freeze with p ≠ q before citing it.

Re-frozen 2026-09-23 with p ≠ q (knowledge/solved/Erdos649.json → refrozen): the (2, 7) proof needed one extra argument, compiles sorry-free on the standard axioms, the trivial p = q route no longer typechecks, and a fresh faithfulness judgment (Opus 5.5, told about the re-freeze) calls it faithful: adding p ≠ q strengthens the negated claim and is the only non-degenerate reading. Operator correction, mechanically re-verified; still needs independent human review like every solve.

Sharp obstruction derived and checked 2026-09-11 (knowledge/reductions/699 addendum): if a prime p>j divides any of n,n-1,...,n-i+1 then n mod p = t < i < j, so the single-digit Kummer lemma applies twice and p divides BOTH binomials with p>j>i. Hence a counterexample forces the descending product n(n-1)...(n-i+1) to be j-SMOOTH. Confirmed over 2,559,266 (n,i,j,p) witnesses for n<400. Strictly stronger than the known 'no prime in (n-i,n]' form, which is just the case where n-t is itself prime.

i=2 is settled outright and elementarily: pi(1)=0 gives V_2(n)=C(n,2), so a counterexample would force C(n,2) | C(j,2) hence n<=j, contradicting 2j<=n. The three known i=2 entries are failures of the strict p>i variant only. For i>=3 the size bound n<=j^(i/(i-pi(i-1))) closes nothing on its own -- the region is an infinite family -- so what must become effective is the smoothness condition, which is precisely the Bugeaud-Evertse-Gyory input the Van Doorn/Rocca manuscript uses ineffectively.

For even n, n=2^r*a (a odd), c=2^r*gcd(a,3), e=gcd(n-1,3); coprime cancellation forces 4(n-1)<=e*c^2<=9*4^r. This is a finite bound only for fixed v2(n), not a full resolution. (U3) uses no Lucas digit above the p^e block and has NO solution for any n with v_2(n)<=30, hence none below 2^31 (parametrised exact search, i3_param2.py; direct brute force to 3e5 agrees). So Conjecture U(3) -- (U3) is unsatisfiable -- would settle i=3; it is a statement about three consecutive integers with no binomial coefficients in it. ---
problem: 699
updated: 2026-09-12
run: 20260911-195529-727426-erdos699
outcome: partial
solved: false
certified: 10
search_floor: 4.17e+19
cost_usd: 30.54

## What the problem asks

For any n and positions 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n/2, must the two binomial coefficients C(n,i) and C(n,j) share a prime factor at least i? A binomial coefficient counts choices of a given size. The prime is allowed to equal i. The full statement remains unproved here.

## What we tried

The inherited research run ended with a session-limit failure in the positive direction and partial results in the negative direction. Its aggregate records contain 10 certified declaration names, 54 model calls, 83 Lean checks, and $30.54 spend. Those counts describe the harness run, not the later operator-assisted continuation. No additional paid harness calls were launched by Codex; Codex session cost is unavailable. The existing published search floor of roughly 4.17 × 10^19 candidate triples was preserved; it was not rerun.

Codex continued directly in Lean using Mathlib's Lucas theorem. Claude repaired one failed proof tactic and moved the results into a shared binomial-coefficient library. This was assisted work, not an autonomous resolution.

## What we found

The carry lemma and the stronger reduction are mechanically verified: if any number among n,n−1,…,n−i+1 has a prime factor greater than j, that prime divides both binomial coefficients. Therefore a counterexample would force every prime factor of every number in that block to be at most j. This property is called j-smoothness. It is a necessary condition for a counterexample, not a proof that counterexamples are impossible.

The proposed next route, Conjecture D, is false at (10,3,5). These binomial coefficients are 120 and 252; the shared prime 3 satisfies #699 but is missed by the proposed units-digit test. The test remains useful as a sufficient condition. It can also find primes between i and j, as p=5 at (16,3,7) demonstrates; only the narrower block-prime argument requires p>j.

A later direct argument for i=3 rules out odd n and gives n ≤ (9/4)·4^r+1 for even n, where r counts factors of two in n. Its intermediate numerical checks passed, but it is a written argument for review, not a new Lean-certified result: the separate formal check timed out. It leaves r unbounded and does not address i≥4. Details are in experiments/699-higher-carries/REPORT.md.

## What would move it

First audit and finish formalizing the written i=3 localization argument; the prior Lean check timed out. Next bring n−2 into the simultaneous constraints from n and n−1, retaining higher-digit carries and the prime p=i=3. Seek a contradiction valid for every r=v₂(n), or prove an absolute cutoff with a feasible exhaustive check. If this route fails, record the exact obstruction before another research run. A bounded check of r cannot settle the unbounded argument; completing i=3 still leaves i≥4.

The harness automatically includes these next steps from atlas-data/research-guidance/699.md in its research and proof prompts, including resumed runs. Reuse the certified BinomialCoefficients library, reject the refuted Conjecture D, and preserve the published search floor. Full details and the distinction between certified results and drafts are in the linked research guidance and experiment reports.

problems.statement: Is there a covering system all of whose moduli are of the form $p-1$ for some primes $p\geq 5$?
rationale: Statement disambiguation: the site's bare wording omits 'distinct'. Erdos-Graham [ErGr80] and google-deepmind/formal-conjectures (StrictCoveringSystem, injective_moduli) both require DISTINCT moduli; without that the problem is trivially YES (0,1,2,3 mod 4, and 4=5-1). Any formalisation without injective moduli is unfaithful.

Parity reduction (self-derived, verified numerically): every allowed modulus p-1 is even, so a congruence class with even residue lies wholly in the evens and one with odd residue wholly in the odds. Halving turns the problem into: find TWO DISJOINT distinct-modulus covering systems with moduli drawn from H = {m>=2 : 2m+1 prime}.

Self-verified lcm floor: if L' is the lcm of the halved moduli then f(L') = sum over d|L', 2d+1 prime, of 1/d must be >= 2 (each of the two disjoint families needs reciprocal sum >= 1). A divisor sieve to 3e6 gives min{L' : f(L') >= 2} = 27720, so the lcm of the original moduli is at least 55440, and only 29 candidate values of L' are <= 200000.

Exhaustive elimination of the 29 candidate lcms below 200000 by DFS (residues forced by covering the least uncovered point, pruned on combined remaining density vs unused reciprocal budget) is INCONCLUSIVE: the tree exceeds 3e6 nodes per candidate. Neither found nor eliminated by this route.

Constructive search is not close. Randomized reciprocal-balanced splits of the divisor pool followed by a greedy ascending build, on the three richest candidates (L'=3603600/2162160/3243240, budgets 2.30/2.29/2.28, 230-343 restarts each), leave 11.7-12.3 percent of the two cyclic groups uncovered at best. A SINGLE covering system from H is easy to build greedily; the obstruction is entirely the disjointness, because the density sits in the small moduli 2,3,5,6,8,9,11 that only one of the two families can hold.

Open, and both directions resist. The parity reduction (all moduli p-1 are even, so residues split by parity) makes it exactly TWO DISJOINT covering systems with distinct moduli drawn from H={m>=2 : 2m+1 prime}; the reciprocal budget over any smooth lcm below 4e6 tops out at 2.30, leaving ~0.15 slack per system, so a witness is cramped but not excluded. A harness run reached only lcm<=55439, which is one below the first numerically viable candidate (55440=2*27720) - i.e. it stopped exactly where the search starts being hard.

stage_reduce found and CHECKED three structural reductions, two of them new to us: (a) the parity decomposition - all moduli p-1 are even, so a solution is exactly TWO covering systems with disjoint moduli drawn from H2={(p-1)/2}; (b) no admissible modulus is 2 mod 6, since m=2 mod 3 forces 3|p, so 8,14,20,26,... are excluded and the standard 2,4,8,16 doubling chain is blocked at its second step; (c) any solution needs at least 18 congruences, because the 17 smallest elements of H2 have reciprocal sum 1.99835 < 2, which also gives a mid-search rejection filter (sum of 2/m must reach 2, not sum of 1/m reach 1).

CORRECTION (2026-09-11): previously scored 6, below #677's 7, which contradicted the assessment. On the axis score actually measures - is a COMPLETE proof mechanically reachable - #273 is the stronger of the two: its affirmative side is a finite certificate at a reachable size (29 candidate lcms up to 393120), so a solver returning SAT at any one of them resolves the problem outright. #677 has no reachable route in either direction. The earlier 6-vs-7 reflected #677's already-banked partial value, which belongs on the partial axis, not this one.

Candidate ordering matters more than candidate size. slack(L) = sum of 1/m over admissible divisors minus 1 bounds the unused reciprocal weight, so every modulus with 1/m > slack is FORCED. L=55440 is the smallest of the 29 candidates but among the loosest (slack 0.0437, only 7 of 43 forced); three attempts were spent on it for that reason alone. L=100800 is the uniquely collapsible one: slack 0.000089, 45 of 50 forced, 5 free, overlap budget 9 points, and only 12 of 32 free subsets reach coverage. Two of those 12 have overlap exactly 0 and are excluded by Mirsky-Newman/Davenport-Rado (a disjoint covering system must repeat its largest modulus, so distinct moduli admit no exact cover) - the first cases on this problem eliminated by a theorem rather than a timer.

The generating-function condition is now derived and validated, not a hunch. For every divisibility-maximal modulus m in the chosen set, L/m <= overlap - because at a primitive m-th root of unity only that term has a pole, giving |sum over the excess multiset of zeta^r| = L/m exactly. Checked to 1e-15 on a known cover with two maximal moduli. It subsumes Mirsky-Newman (overlap 0 demands L/m <= 0) and cuts L=100800's 12 coverage-reaching subsets to 7 in milliseconds, where a SAT encoding of ONE subset did not decide in 37 minutes. Standard argument, no novelty claimed.

FIBRE/FOURIER ELIMINATION (2026-09-11, $0, no model calls): for every d|L and primitive d-th root of unity zeta, sum over m in U with d|m of (L/m)zeta^{a_m} equals the zeta-transform of the excess, so its modulus is at most k = sum L/m - L. Reverse triangle inequality gives a residue-free screen 2*max(W)-sum(W) > k. This ELIMINATES 20 of the 29 candidate lcm values below 400000, including BOTH candidates that consumed every previous attempt: L=55440 (three attempts, margin 2437 vs k<=2421) and L=100800 (two attempts, 1903 vs k<=9). Four solver runs timed out on those two; the test decides both in under a millisecond.

Search floor advances from a SCREEN at 55440 to EXHAUSTIVE at 110880 - every candidate below that is now excluded by proof. Surviving candidates below 400000: 110880, 166320, 221760, 262080, 277200, 302400, 332640, 388080, 393120, all loose (slack 0.02-0.08, k in the thousands) where the inequality has no bite. The 400000 cap is compute, not a theorem.

The test bites hardest exactly where a candidate looks most attractive: k <= slack*L, so the tiny-slack candidates chosen for being nearly determined have almost no excess budget. m=16 does most of the work (17 prime, so 16 is admissible and forced) while the other admissible multiples of 16 are too sparse to cancel its weight. Standard Mirsky-Newman style argument applied at every d rather than only the largest modulus; no novelty of technique claimed.

FOLLOW-UP (2026-09-11): the fibre/Fourier family is now provably EXHAUSTED, by decision rather than by search. Every d-constraint is implied by the constraint at mu = min{m in U : d|m}, so the family collapses to: for every mu in U, L/mu - sum_{m in U, mu|m, m!=mu} L/m <= k_U. That form is monotone in U, so a mu violating it under the maximal admissible set violates under every subset containing it and can be deleted outright; iterating to a fixed point is COMPLETE in polynomial time. No 2^47 enumeration is needed.

Propagation eliminates exactly the same 20 candidates and deletes ZERO moduli at all nine survivors - the full admissible set already satisfies every constraint there, so no subset search can improve on it. The survivors fall short by 1944 to 19326; the closest, L=302400, misses by 1944 against a budget of 6700 (a 29 percent gap), versus 55440 which is over by only 16. Regression: 3130 genuine covering systems built across L=12..720, zero false kills.

The reason is intrinsic: k <= slack*L, so the inequality bites exactly when slack is tiny. The 20 eliminated are the tight candidates; the nine survivors all have slack 0.02-0.08 and thousands of units of excess to absorb any imbalance. ## What the problem asks

A "covering system" is a finite list of rules like "numbers that leave remainder 3 when divided by 8". Each rule has a divisor, called its modulus, and a remainder. The list covers if every whole number, positive or negative, obeys at least one rule. The question asks whether such a list exists when every modulus is one less than a prime number of at least 5 — so the allowed moduli are 4, 6, 10, 12, 16, 18, and so on. The moduli must all be different; reusing a modulus with a new remainder is not allowed. This problem is open on the published catalogue. Nobody knows the answer, yes or no.

## What we tried

One automated run in search-first mode, costing $12.84, which found nothing and produced no certified results. Three earlier attempts had all attacked the same candidate size and all timed out. After that run, a hand analysis costing nothing — no model calls, milliseconds of computation — replaced the search with an algebraic test. Every modulus in such a list must divide one number, the least common multiple, and only 29 values of that number below 400,000 are even arithmetically possible. The test asks, for each one, whether the rules could fit together at all, without ever choosing remainders.

## What we found

**Twenty of the 29 possible sizes are impossible.** The argument counts how much the rules overlap. Sort the whole numbers into groups by their remainder when divided by some number `d`. A rule whose modulus is a multiple of `d` sits inside a single group; every other rule spreads evenly across groups and cancels out when you weigh the groups against each other. So the imbalance between groups has to be paid for entirely out of the overlap — the amount by which the rules double-cover. When the arithmetic is tight, there is almost no overlap to spend, and one heavy rule cannot be balanced.

The two sizes that had consumed all five previous attempts, 55,440 and 100,800, both fail this way in under a millisecond. For 100,800 the overlap can be at most 9, while the imbalance is at least 1,903. Four solver runs had previously failed to settle these two, one of them running 37 minutes without an answer.

**So no such list exists with least common multiple below 110,880** — and that is now settled by proof rather than by a filter, which is what the previous record at 55,440 was.

The test is also provably finished. Its tightest form can be decided completely, without trying combinations, and on the nine remaining sizes it rules out nothing at all: those sizes have loose arithmetic, leaving thousands of units of overlap to absorb any imbalance. The nearest miss, 302,400, falls short by 1,944. This is not a matter of searching harder.

The same test was checked against 3,130 genuine covering systems built by hand and never wrongly rejected one, and the two closest calls were recomputed in exact fractions rather than decimals.

## What would move it

Only a witness, or an argument that works for all sizes at once. The nine remaining candidates need a satisfiability solver — software that decides whether a set of constraints can be met — and they are harder targets than the ones already tried, being both larger and looser. The list of 29 stops at 400,000 because that is where the computation stopped, not because of any theorem, so a covering system could exist at a far larger size. **This work removed candidates; it did not answer the question, and it made the remaining ones look worse rather than better.**

problems.statement: Let $r\geq 3$. If the edges of $K_{r^2+1}$ are $r$-coloured then there exist $r+1$ vertices with at least one colour missing on the edges of the induced $K_{r+1}$.
rationale: Each fixed r is a finite, SAT-encodable decision problem; r=3 and r=4 are published (Erdos-Gyarfas) and the claims page carries verification programs for r=5,7,8,9.

EVERY REACHABLE FIXED CASE IS ALREADY CLAIMED (recorded 2026-09-11 from the proof-claims page, claims NOT verified by us). Seven proof claims filed in July 2026, all AI-assisted and all partial: r=5 independently four times (Winter, Rose, Silverstein, Sneiderman - with 458 DRAT-verified SAT leaves, twelve UNSAT formulas, and Kang-Pikhurko equality routes), plus r=6 (K_37), r=7 (K_50), r=8 (K_65, 862 LRAT-checked instances) and r=9 (K_82, 50 LRAT certificates). Erdos-Gyarfas published r=3 and r=4. So the first UNCLAIMED fixed case is r=10 (K_101, 5050 edges), and the universal statement over all r is what remains genuinely open.

The thread identifies the problem as equivalent to R^r_{r-1}(K_{r+1}) <= r^2+1, a named quantity in the weakened-Ramsey and complementary-Ramsey literatures (Chung-Liu 1978 Theorem 3.6 gives R^3_2(K_4,K_4,K_4)=10, i.e. the r=3 case, 21 years before [ErGy99]; Harborth-Moller 1999; Munemasa-Shinohara). Equality holds whenever the affine plane of order r exists - which for r=10 it does NOT (Lam-Thiel-Swiercz), so r=10 may behave differently from the prime-power ladder.
Crowded: seven users listed as currently working on it. A harness run would be competing for the one remaining reachable case against teams that produced four independent r=5 proofs in a week.

problems.statement: The independent set sequence of any tree or forest is unimodal. In other words, if $i_k(G)$ counts the number of independent sets of vertices of size $k$ in a graph $G$, and $T$ is any tree or forest, then for some $m\geq 0$ $$i_{0}(T)\leq i_{1}(T)\leq\cdots\leq i_{m}(T)\geq i_{m+1}(T)\geq i_{m+2}(T)\geq\cdots.$$
rationale: EXHAUSTIVELY VERIFIED TO n=32 by third parties (recorded 2026-09-11 from the forum thread, NOT rerun by us). All 109,972,410,221 free trees on 32 vertices checked with nauty/gentreeg plus an exact integer in/out subtree DP, zero unimodality failures, per-order counts matching OEIS A000055 end-to-end; n=30 and n=31 (14.8e9 and 40.3e9 trees) were done by two independent implementations in full agreement. A bounded tree search re-derives known ground - n=33 is ~300 billion trees.

The structural frontier is also moving: every spider has a strongly log-concave independence polynomial (Li-Li-Yang-Zhang), and a thread contributor extends this to every tree with at most two vertices of degree >= 3, so any counterexample needs at least three such vertices. For the 'or forest' half, Hoggar's theorem means a forest can only fail if a tree component is already non-log-concave, and the smallest such tree has 26 vertices (Kadrawi-Levit).

FLOOR UNIT (corrected 2026-09-11): recorded as 1.1e11 ENUMERABLE OBJECTS - the 109,972,410,221 free trees on 32 vertices actually checked - not as the parameter n=32. A floor is compared against SEARCH_REACH, which counts objects a bounded search can enumerate, so a floor filed in parameter units (32) would read as 'cheap' and let the gate run a search that is in fact 11 orders of magnitude out of reach. Cumulative verification is n <= 32.

problem: 455
updated: 2026-10-02
run: 20261001-230105-000000-erdos455
outcome: partial
solved: false
certified: 2
cost_usd: 18.99

## What the problem asks

A prime is a whole number above 1 that only 1 and itself divide evenly, such as 2, 3, 5 or 7. Take an endless list of primes in increasing order, q_1 < q_2 < …. A gap is the difference between one prime in the list and the next. The rule is that gaps never shrink: each gap is at least as big as the one before. The question is whether such a list must outgrow every fixed multiple of n², the square of a prime's position n in the list. Put another way: must q_n divided by n² eventually pass every number? The catalogue lists the problem as open. It also says no finite computation can settle it.

## What we tried

This was a research run: an automated attempt to build a proof by splitting the problem into smaller claims, each checked by Lean, a program that verifies proofs step by step. Before any Lean work, a discovery stage wrote twelve informal attempts in three independent draws. Every attempt judged the answer "yes", so the run worked only toward "yes". None of them was a complete proof that the automatic referee accepted.

The run was allowed six cycles of planning and proving. It ran three, then stopped, because two cycles in a row settled nothing new. When the one hard claim failed in Lean, the harness tried a fresh informal attack on that claim alone. It told that attack what Lean had already proved. This found no proof either. The cost was $18.99 of a $40 cap. A human chose the problem and the settings. The exact statement came from formal-conjectures, an outside collection of formal statements. The run was also given summaries of six papers and the problem's forum discussion. It was given no proof ideas beyond those.

## What we found

The problem is not solved. Lean certified two facts, and both passed the project's checks: the proof was re-checked by Lean's kernel, it uses only the standard axioms, and it has no unfinished steps.

- **The gap bound.** Take any finite run of primes whose gaps never shrink. Then the i-th gap is at least i/6. Adding the gaps up shows that q_n is at least about n²/12, so q_n/n² can never fall below roughly 1/12. Richter proved a stronger version of this in 1976, with 0.352 in place of 1/12. So this is a machine-checked proof of a weaker form of a known result, not new mathematics.
- **A bridge.** If the gaps never shrink, the distance from q_k to q_n is at least (n − k) times the gap at k.

With these, the problem reduces to one claim. Fix any number C. For large n, there is no run of about n/2 primes below C·n² whose gaps never shrink and stay at most 2Cn. This claim is as hard as the problem itself. The harness tried three times to split it into easier pieces. Each time, a separate automatic judge pointed out that the pieces were the same claim in new words, because the gap bound already supplies the extra conditions for free.

## What would move it

The missing step is a proof that the gaps skip almost every even number. Among the even numbers up to x, the ones that actually occur as gaps must be a vanishing fraction as x grows. That would take a sieve, meaning a counting method strong enough to bound long, nearly square-shaped patterns of primes uniformly. The informal attempts also suggest that tricks based only on a few fixed small primes cannot work; this was not checked. A future run starts from this run's notes, kept in the problem's campaign blackboard.

*Corrected by hand on 2026-10-02 from the automatic brief of run `20261001-230105-000000-erdos455`. The automatic version said six cycles had run, where three ran, and it left out the gap bound. A machine-checked proof certifies the statement it names, not the problem. Nothing here has had independent human review.*

problems.statement: Can every integer $N\geq 2$ be written as\[N=\frac{\prod_{1\leq i\leq k}(m+i)}{\prod_{1\leq i\leq k}(n+i)}\]for some $k\geq 2$ and $m\geq n+k$?

For squares, N = 4, 25, 49, 64, 81 are the open values below 100: not representable for k <= 4 (k=4 reduces to k=2), excluded at k=3 for N = 4, 49, 64 via Chan's method with Bennett's irrationality measures (vilc), and Kovac's root-expansion trick excludes N=4 and N=64 at k=6; 25 and 81 at k=3 and everything at k >= 5 are open. Quanyu Tang conjectures N = p^2 (p >= 5 prime) is never representable. Finiteness for fixed N and k >= 3 is known (Beukers-Shorey-Tijdeman / Rakaczki) but ineffective for k >= 4.

problems.statement: Is there a distinct covering system all of whose moduli are odd?
rationale: The odd-covering-system question remains hard despite its finite-certificate label and known restrictions on moduli.

PUBLISHED SEARCH FLOOR (recorded 2026-09-11, NOT rerun by us): a preprint linked from the #7 forum thread (egeozturk, 18 Aug 2026, 'Closed-form nonexistence certificates for odd covering systems') claims no covering system with distinct odd moduli > 1 has lcm below 11,486,475, by a search-free hierarchy of closed-form certificates in exact rational arithmetic - extending an earlier search-based 2e6 computation. UNREFEREED preprint, self-described as undergraduate work, not verified by us. Its own stated stopping point is the strongly abundant smooth moduli, first uncertified case 11486475 = 3^3*5^2*7*11*13*17.

Our fibre/Fourier test (see #273, knowledge/reductions/273/) transfers to #7 verbatim - every divisor m>1 of odd L is admissible, the reciprocal screen becomes 'L is ODD ABUNDANT' (smallest 945), and the condition collapses to: max over n|L, n<L of (2n - sigma(n)) <= sigma(L) - 2L. It eliminates 191 of the 391 candidates below 200,000 (including 945: 58 > 30 at n=189) and gives a floor of 3,465. ## What the problem asks

Take a run of whole numbers, say the k numbers just after n: n+1, n+2, up to n+k. Their "least common multiple" is the smallest number that every one of them divides into evenly. Call it M(n,k). The question, from Erdős, is whether this value can ever repeat: if you slide the run far enough along the number line so the new run starts at or beyond n+k (that is, m ≥ n+k, so the two runs do not overlap), must the least common multiple always be different? The problem is listed as open on the problem catalogue, and remains open. Nothing here changes that.

## What we tried

We ran the harness in research mode on the problem, with some context supplied by the operator. Two directions were pursued: trying to prove the statement, and trying to break it by finding one concrete example of a repeat. The proving direction hit an infrastructure error and produced nothing usable. The disproving direction returned partial progress. Alongside the run, an earlier assessment had already reduced the question to more tractable pieces and swept ranges of numbers by computer looking for a repeat. Twelve small side results were written out and machine-checked in the Lean proof system, which verifies each step mechanically. The run cost $34.25 and recorded four infrastructure failures.

## What we found

No repeat was found, and no proof was produced. The two easiest cases, k = 1 and k = 2 (runs of one or two numbers), are settled by elementary reasoning: there the least common multiple simply grows as you slide along, so it cannot repeat. The general case is untouched. A computer sweep found no example anywhere it looked; the recorded search bound is 1,000,000,000, and its recorded kind is exhaustive, meaning every case in that range was actually enumerated. For the k = 3 case the whole question collapses to one equation in two unknowns, and the only solution found in the swept range involves overlapping runs, which the statement permits. Repeats do occur, but only for runs that overlap by a small gap.

## What would move it

Two routes. To break the statement, someone needs one explicit triple of numbers (n, k, m) with the runs not overlapping and the two least common multiples equal. Our evidence says not to look by brute force: the swept ranges are empty and the structure found there suggests a bounded search is close to futile. To prove it, someone needs a general argument that works for every run length k at once. The known number-theory tools give results only for one fixed k at a time, and even k = 3 already turns into a hard equation-solving problem. Worth formalising meanwhile: the k ≤ 2 cases, a periodicity fact, and a smoothness fact. Those are side results, not the problem.

## What the problem asks

Take any whole number n larger than 2. The question is whether 4/n can always be written as a sum of three fractions of the form 1/x, where x is a whole number and the three x's are all different. Such a fraction, with 1 on top, is called a unit fraction. For example, 4/3 = 1/1 + 1/4 + 1/12. The catalogue lists the problem as open and "falsifiable". That means a single number n with no such sum would disprove it. The claim must hold for every n, and nobody has shown that it does.

## What we tried

We ran an automated research program in two directions. One direction tried to prove the claim. The other tried to find a number n where it fails. Each direction splits the goal into smaller statements. It tries to settle each one and passes the rest to the next cycle. Both directions stopped after 2 cycles because no further piece could be settled. The small results were checked in Lean. Lean is a computer system that verifies proofs line by line. The formal version reads n as a whole number and treats the equation as exact arithmetic with fractions. These are the standard readings. No outside help was recorded. The run cost $15.94.

## What we found

This work is partial. The problem is not solved. The most useful reduction is this: if 4/p has a sum for a prime p, then so does 4/n for every multiple n of p. A prime is a number whose only divisors are 1 and itself. Explicit formulas then handle every prime except those leaving remainder 1 when divided by 24. Eight lemmas were certified, meaning checked in Lean. They cover several of these formula families. An earlier note on the same day also records extra families based on remainders when divided by 840 and by 11. One open statement remains. It is the hard core of the problem. The summary reduction statements were written in Lean but not proved there. No counterexample was found.

## What would move it

The run searched for no new numbers. A published check, which we did not rerun, reports that the claim holds for all n up to 10^18. So a counterexample search within reach is not useful. Notes on the problem suggest certifying more of the known published formula families. That would shrink the remaining open case further. It would still not solve the problem. A full answer needs one of two things. The first is one formula that covers all remaining primes. The second is an actual counterexample beyond the checked range. The counterexample stage failed in every cycle of an earlier run on this problem. It has since been fixed, so later runs should use the working version.

## What the problem asks

Take n points on a flat plane. They must follow one rule: if you draw a circle centred on any one of the points, that circle passes through at most two of the other points. Now measure the distance between every pair of points and count how many different lengths appear. The question asks whether that count is always noticeably more than half of n. "Noticeably more" means at least (1+c) times n/2, for some fixed positive number c, once n is large enough. In plain terms, the question is whether the rule forces many different distances, beyond a basic minimum.

## What we tried

This run worked in research mode and cost $0.82. It used Lean, a computer program that checks every step of a proof mechanically. It worked with a fixed formal version of the question written in Lean. It tried to prove that this formal version is false. No computer search over examples was done, and none was needed. Two earlier Lean attempts on 2026-10-14 did not finish. Before that, an informal written argument had been accepted by a referee, an adversary and two judges. An earlier model put the chance of settling the question at 0.88. That figure is an unvalidated estimate made before any work began.

## What we found

Lean accepted a complete proof that the formal version, as written, is false. The proof relies on no unproven assumptions. The example is the regular polygon: n points spaced evenly around a circle, for any n of 3 or more. These points obey the rule, because a circle centred at one of them crosses the polygon's circle in at most two places. Yet they produce only about n/2 different distances, since opposite steps around the polygon give equal lengths. ## What the problem asks

Take a cube in n dimensions, where n is the number of directions it extends in. Can you cut it exactly into k smaller cubes? Here every piece must be a shrunken copy of the big cube, sitting square to it. Mathematicians call such copies "homothetic". For some values of k this cannot be done. Let c(n) be the smallest number such that every k from c(n) upward works. The question asks for good estimates of c(n). In particular, is c(n) always at least some fixed fraction of n^n, which is n multiplied by itself n times? That is the meaning of the symbol "≫" here.

## What we tried

This run worked toward the "no" answer. The goal was to show c(n) can grow more slowly than any fixed fraction of n^n. The work was done in Lean, which is software that checks each step of a proof mechanically. The plan split the argument into 13 smaller claims, called hypotheses. All 13 were marked as dealt with. Twelve were certified, meaning Lean accepted their proofs. The thirteenth, named `erdos_769_neg_hyp_noCommon`, is not on the certified list. The overall structure fit together. But the final check of the whole proof did not pass. So the "no" direction is recorded as proved but unverified. The run cost $6.69.

## What we found

The problem has **not** been solved. The most useful finding is a step that removes the geometry. Two moves are possible. You can cut the cube into a grid of a^n equal smaller cubes. You can also replace any one piece with a scaled copy of a full cutting. So k = 1 plus any sum of numbers of the form a^n − 1 always works. What remains is pure arithmetic about which totals such sums can reach. A related step says that for odd n ≥ 253, no whole number above 1 divides all of 2^n − 1, 3^n − 1, and so on up to (n/4 + 1)^n − 1. That was checked by computer only for odd n from 253 to 1801. These steps were checked by hand. In Lean they were stated but not proved. No search bound was recorded.

## What would move it

The final verification must pass. Someone needs to find why the full proof failed the last check even though its parts fit together. The uncertified hypothesis, `noCommon`, needs a proof that Lean accepts. It is the claim that no number above 1 divides all of the a^n − 1 values. The stated arithmetic steps also need real Lean proofs, since they now rest on placeholders. Separately, an earlier informal attempt, not part of this run, wrote a full "no" answer. Reviewers accepted it, and it was sent to Lean. A finished, verified Lean proof would be needed before calling the question settled.

problems.statement: If $n=\prod_{1\leq i\leq t} p_i^{k_i}$ is the factorisation of $n$ into distinct primes then let\[f(n)=\sum p_i^{\ell_i},\]where $\ell_i$ is chosen such that $n\in [p_i^{\ell_i},p_i^{\ell_i+1})$. Furthermore, let\[F(n)=\max \sum_{i} a_i\]where the maximum is taken over all distinct $a_1,\ldots,a_k\leq n$ such that $(a_i,a_j)=1$ for $i\neq j$ and all prime factors of each $a_i$ are prime factors of $n$. Is it true that, for almost all $n$,\[f(n)=o(n\log\log n)\]and\[F(n) \gg n\log\log n?\]Is it true that\[\max_{n\leq x}f(n)\sim \frac{x\log x}{\log\log x}?\]Is it true that (for all $x$, or perhaps just for all large $x$)\[\max_{n\leq x}f(n)=\max_{n\leq x}F(n)?\]Find an asymptotic formula for the number of $n<x$ such that $f(n)=F(n)$. Find an asymptotic formula for\[H(x)=\sum_{n<x}\frac{f(n)}{n}.\]Is it true that\[H(x) \ll x\log\log\log\log x?\]
